cards.front: A {{c1::population}} is every member of one species in one area at one time.
cards.quote: A population is every member of one species in one area at one time.

cards.front: {{c1::Land use}} means how people use land: for farms, homes, roads or forest.
cards.quote: Land use means how people use land: for farms, homes, roads or forest.

cards.front: {{c1::Pollution}} is harmful material added to air, water or soil.
cards.quote: Pollution is harmful material added to air, water or soil.

cards.front: What is habitat destruction? Give one example.
cards.back: It removes or ruins habitat. Filling a marsh is an example.
cards.quote: Habitat destruction removes or ruins habitat, such as filling a marsh.

cards.front: What makes a species invasive, and is being new to a place enough?
cards.back: An invasive species is brought to a new place, spreads and causes harm to native species or people. Being new is not enough.
cards.quote: An invasive species is brought to a new place, spreads and causes harm to native species or people; being new is not enough.
cards.section: Explain: a new fish and shared food

cards.front: What is a native species?
cards.back: A species that lives in a place naturally, without people bringing it.
cards.quote: A native species lives in a place naturally, without people bringing it.
cards.section: Explain: a new fish and shared food

cards.front: State the one rule to carry through the lesson about people and ecosystems.
cards.back: When people change an ecosystem, populations may rise or fall. It does not predict which population will change or prove the cause of a survey pattern.
cards.quote: When people change an ecosystem, populations may rise or fall.

cards.front: Why do local populations often drop when a marsh is filled in?
cards.back: The animals there lose their habitat, so they must move or die.
cards.quote: Animals there must move or die, so local populations often drop.

cards.front: How can farm fertilizer end up harming fish in a river?
cards.back: Rain carries it into streams. The extra fertilizer feeds fast algae growth, and later the water can run low on oxygen.
cards.why: The lesson links extra fertilizer to fast algae growth and, later, low oxygen.
cards.quote: Rain can carry fertilizer and manure from farm fields into streams.

cards.front: Why can one change in a food web make some populations rise and others fall?
cards.back: A food web links species by who eats whom, so a change in one species spreads to the species connected to it.
cards.quote: so one change can spread: some populations go up, and others go down.

cards.front: Blue catfish and white catfish eat similar prey. Why might they compete even if they never fight?
cards.back: Competition means needing the same limited resource, such as food or space. A new species can eat food the native one needs.
cards.quote: Scientists report that the two catfish eat similar prey, so they may compete.
cards.section: Explain: a new fish and shared food

cards.front: In the James River catfish survey, what does a survey index tell you, and what does it not tell you?
cards.back: It tracks how common a fish is in the surveyed area from year to year. It is not a count of every fish.
cards.quote: It tracks how common a fish is in the surveyed area from year to year.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the James River surveys

cards.front: Why can you not compare the blue catfish index and the white catfish index number to number?
cards.back: The two indexes use different math and river areas, so compare each fish only with itself.
cards.quote: Compare each fish only with itself, because the two indexes use different math and river areas.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the James River surveys

cards.front: Give one example of a human effect on an ecosystem that was not negative.
cards.back: People spread eelgrass seeds in Virginia's coastal bays. A 2020 study reported that underwater grass returned and the total mass of fish rose.
cards.quote: A 2020 study reported that underwater grass returned and the total mass of fish rose

cards.front: Heavy fishing removes many blue catfish from a model river with limited food shared with white catfish. Predict what happens to the white catfish bar and why.
cards.back: It may rise. Fewer blue catfish means more shared prey is left for white catfish. This rests on the rule that fewer competitors can leave more food, though a model only shows possible effects.
cards.quote: A model shows possible effects, not what caused a change in a real river.

cards.front: If blue catfish eat many blue crabs, predict what happens to the other animals and people that eat blue crabs, and why.
cards.back: Fewer crabs may remain for them. Crab eaters share one limited food supply.
cards.quote: If blue catfish eat many blue crabs, fewer may remain for other crab eaters, including people.
cards.section: Explain: a new fish and shared food

cards.front: A town builds homes on a filled-in coastal marsh. Predict what happens to the crabs and birds that lived there, and name the kind of disruption.
cards.back: Their local populations will likely drop. This is habitat destruction: the food, water and shelter they need are gone.
cards.quote: Habitat destruction, pollution and invasive species are three ways people disrupt ecosystems.

cards.front: In the James River survey, the white catfish index fell from 1.31 in 1995 to 0.16 in 2022. By about what percent did it fall?
cards.quote: Then calculate: subtract, divide by 1.31 and multiply by 100.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the James River surveys

cards.front: The blue catfish index was 8.97 in 1995 and 54.42 in 2022. About how many times larger was the 2022 index?
cards.back: 54.42 / 8.97 is about 6.1, so about six times the 1995 index. This shows a pattern, not its cause.
cards.quote: So the 2022 blue index was about six times the 1995 index. That is a pattern, not its cause.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the James River surveys

cards.front: The ten blue catfish index values sum to 568.70, and 2019 is 317.77. What is the mean with and without 2019, and what does that show?
cards.back: With 2019: 568.70 / 10 = 56.87. Without: 250.93 / 9 is about 27.9. One year can roughly double the mean.
cards.quote: Find the mean of the blue values with and without 2019.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the James River surveys

cards.front: Design a fair test with soil trays: does a plant strip keep soil out of a creek? Name the variables and controls.
cards.back: Independent: a grass-sod strip 10 cm wide at the low end, or bare soil. Dependent: runoff soil mass in grams. Control: bare-soil trays. Constants: same soil, tray, tilt and 1 liter of water. Three trays of each kind; find each mean.
cards.quote: Plan a test with soil trays: does a plant strip keep soil out of the creek?

cards.front: In the James River surveys, blue catfish rose while white catfish fell. What claim can you make, and what can you not claim?
cards.back: Claim: blue catfish became more common while native white catfish became rarer. Similar prey makes competition possible, but the survey shows a pattern, not the cause.
cards.why: Land use, habitat destruction and pollution can also change populations.
cards.quote: Similar prey makes competition possible, even without a fight, but the survey shows a pattern, not its cause.
